claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are chemically homogeneous.
Heating induces nanoscale chemical partitioning in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Copper is a lower-melting-point constituent of the nanoparticle system.
Lower-melting-point elements segregate locally during heating.
Local enrichment in lower-melting-point elements forms premature melting zones.
Moderate heating rates permit atomic diffusion while avoiding non-equilibrium effects.
Atomic mobility under the proposed heating conditions permits detectable elemental segregation.
Nanoscale chemical segregation or local compositional fluctuations arise during heating.
Heating selectively mobilizes elements with lower melting points through atomic diffusion.
Selective elemental mobility produces local enrichment of lower-melting-point components.
Segregated regions enriched in lower-melting-point components have reduced lattice stability.
Reduced lattice stability lowers the local melting point and causes premelting at segregated sites.
A perfectly homogeneous nanoparticle would undergo a more spatially uniform melting transition.
Localized or surface premelting will begin preferentially in regions enriched in lower-melting-point constituents.
Nanoparticles that maintain chemical homogeneity will show uniform melting characteristic of a single phase transition.
The proposed mechanism is limited to nanoparticles of similar size and composition under heating rates that permit diffusion without masking it.
The proposed mechanism is not expected to govern when particle-size effects or surface oxidation dominate melting behavior.
Surface curvature, strain, or incidental oxide formation could contribute to altered melting behavior independently of segregation.
